sentences.text: Pluridens was an extinct marine lizard belonging to the family Mosasauridae, specifically within the subfamily Halisaurinae.
This animal was a moderately large mosasaurid, typically reaching lengths of five to six meters, though some individuals may have grown up to nine meters.
It is distinguished by having almost twice as many teeth in its lower jaws as found in most other members of its group.
The lower jaw bone, known as the dentary, possessed one of the slimmest profiles among all known mosasaurs.
Fossil evidence reveals robust jaws bearing injuries that suggest the animal engaged in physical combat.
Due to the physics of biting force, the front teeth located far from the jaw joint were likely ineffective for crushing prey.
Three species were originally described: P. walkeri from early Maastrichtian Niger, P. calabaria from Campanian Nigeria, and P. serpentis from late Maastrichtian Morocco.
The type specimen for P. walkeri is cataloged as BMNH R14153, representing an almost complete lower jaw recovered from the Farin-Doutchi Formation near Mount Ilatarda.
Longrich named P. calabaria in 2016 because its lower jaw lacked the extreme side bulge and nearly circular cross-section seen in the type specimen.
The third species, P. serpentis, was described in 2021 from phosphate deposits in Morocco and holds the title of the most completely known species with two skulls and several jaws.
A fourth species, P. imelaki, was described in 2026 from Moroccan phosphates based on a single skull and lower jaws.
Researchers suggest the animal may have used its powerful jaws to fight over mates or territories.
Lingham-Soliar compared the lifestyle and feeding habits of Pluridens to early ichthyosaurs like Temnodontosaurus and Leptonectes.
Pluridens is currently classified as a highly derived member of the Halisaurinae subfamily.
Its parent group is the tribe Pluridensini.
The type species of the genus is P. walkeri.
Lindgren and Siverson initially suggested that many unique features were shared with Halisaurus and reclassified P. walkeri as Halisaurus walkeri.
Pluridens lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.

It is debated whether Pluridens is a distinct genus; Lindgren and Siverson synonymized it with Halisaurus, but later authors rejected this synonymy because the unique features warranted a new subfamily, although he did not create one due to the fragmentary nature of the fossil remains.
